slides.title: Unit 1 Overview - Applications of Biology
key_points: Biology helps us understand all living organisms from bacteria to blue whales
Applications include disease control, pest management, drug discovery, and genetic engineering
Biology provides understanding of evolution, extinction rates, and conservation
Practical applications include hand washing, domestication, and traditional fermentation
Biotechnology combines biology and technology for human benefit
slides.notes: This unit explores how biological knowledge is applied in daily life, from disease control to food production and environmental conservation.

slides.title: 1.1 Conservation of Natural Resources
key_points: Conservation: Careful maintenance and wise use of natural resources to prevent them from disappearing
Natural resources: Physical supplies from nature including soil, water, air, plants, animals, and energy
Renewable resources: Can be used, reused, and replaced when managed carefully
Non-renewable resources: Finite resources not replaced at same speed they are used
Ethiopia's natural resources include gold, platinum, potash, limestone, natural gas, coal, lakes, waterfalls, timber, coffee, and diverse species
slides.notes: Natural resources are classified as renewable or non-renewable. Renewable resources (sun, wind, water, biomass) can be used repeatedly when managed well. Non-renewable resources (metals, fossil fuels) are finite and must be used sparingly. Biologists play a key role in conserving species and their habitats.

slides.title: 1.1 Conservation Strategies and Importance
key_points: Conservation prevents disappearance of resources and protects biodiversity
Biologists conserve species and save them from extinction through preservation of natural habitats, zoos, and seed banks
Coppicing and planting trees to replace those cut down ensures sustainable forest management
Using renewable energy sources reduces dependence on non-renewable resources
Ethiopia's renewable resources include Coffee (Coffea arabica), Walia Ibex (Capra walie), and Ethiopian Bush crow (Zavattariornis stresemanni)
slides.notes: Conservation is protecting and preserving our natural environment so that non-renewable resources are used sparingly, and renewable resources are appropriately managed. Without careful management, even renewable resources can be lost.

slides.title: 1.2 Food and Nutrition Security
key_points: Food security: State where all people have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food at all times
Food insecurity is often rooted in poverty and causes long-term impacts on development
Nutrition security: Access to sufficient, safe, nutritious foods, safe water, adequate sanitation, health care, and knowledge of proper practices
Food security requires: enough food available, capacity to buy quality food, and no barriers to access food
Biology produces high-nutrient staple crops and develops new products to combat malnutrition
slides.notes: Prolonged undernourishment stunts growth, slows cognitive development, and increases susceptibility to illness. Food security is ensured only when food is available, accessible, and affordable for all.

slides.title: 1.2 Understanding Food Insecurity
key_points: Food insecurity is often rooted in poverty
Long-term impacts on families, communities, and countries to develop and prosper
Types of malnutrition: Stunting (too short for age), Wasting (too thin for height), Over nutrition (too fat for height and age), Micronutrient deficiencies
Prolonged undernourishment stunts growth, slows cognitive development, and increases susceptibility to illness
Biotechnologists design manufacturing processes for consistent food flavor, color, and texture in large quantities
slides.notes: Food and nutrition insecurity have severe consequences on human development, particularly in children. Biology plays a key role in addressing these challenges through improved crop production and food processing.

slides.title: 1.3 Conscious Citizens and Sustainable Development
key_points: Conscious citizen: Person who places value on being fully human while connecting with a higher purpose
Biology expands awareness of social, global, and environmental conditions
Conscious citizens assume personal responsibility and commit to positive impact
Biotechnology facilitates sustainable development initiatives
Conscious citizen biologists develop innovative, cost-effective bio-based technologies
slides.notes: A conscious citizen values human life and relationship with all living things, taking responsibility for transforming skills into action through ethical decision-making to improve life on the planet.

slides.title: 1.3 Sustainable Development Model
key_points: Three dimensions of sustainability: Economic, Social, and Environmental
Conscious global biologists in Ethiopia involved in protecting, managing, and monitoring existing resources
Activities include: analyzing soil, water, and air for pollution; finding ways to clean up pollution
Identifying, recording, and monitoring plants and animals
Developing technologies that consume fewer resources, incorporate recycling, reduce waste
slides.notes: Sustainable development involves balancing economic, social, and environmental needs. Biology empowers citizens to develop innovative technologies that support a greener earth and improved food production.

slides.title: 1.4 Introduction to Biotechnology
key_points: Biotechnology: Application of technologies using living organisms or their products for human benefit
Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs): Received genetic material via recombinant DNA technology
Transgenic organism: Received genetic material from a different species
Transgene: Gene from one species introduced into another species
Crops can be modified to increase yields and obtain novel products
slides.notes: Biotechnology can be used in food processing, agriculture, medicine, and environmental protection. GMOs have been developed for improved traits and disease resistance.

slides.title: 1.4 Food Processing and Production
key_points: Single-cell protein (SCP): Produced from waste materials like molasses, petroleum by-products, agricultural wastes
Pruteen: Produced by Methylophilus methylotrophus bacteria
Mycoprotein: Produced from Fusarium venenatum fungus, used as meat substitute
Spirulina: Cyanobacterium harvested from lakes, used as nutrient source
Vitamins produced via fermentation: Vitamin C, Vitamin B12, Vitamin B2
Dairy products: Cultured buttermilk (Streptococcus cremoris), Yogurt (Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus)
slides.notes: Microorganisms are essential in food production, from SCP to dairy products. Fermentation processes produce various foods and beverages with specific flavors and textures.

slides.title: 1.4 Beer, Wine, and Bread Production
key_points: Beer and wine: Made by fermenting sugary juices using Saccharomyces strains
Beer making: Malted barley, hops, Saccharomyces fermentation produces ethyl alcohol, CO2, amyl and isoamyl alcohols, acetic and butyric acids
Wine making: Juice treated with sulfur dioxide, Saccharomyces added, fermentation produces ethyl alcohol and other flavor compounds
Spirits (whiskey, gin, rum): Made by fermenting various foods and distilling the product
Bread making: Saccharomyces cerevisiae used for leavening (CO2 production), flavor, and dough conditioning
Lactic acid bacteria contribute to rye and sourdough bread flavors
slides.notes: Yeast strains of Saccharomyces are the fermenters for all alcoholic beverages. Bread making uses yeast for leavening and flavor, with lactic acid bacteria contributing to specialty breads.

slides.title: 1.4 Traditional Ethiopian Fermentation
key_points: Injera: Traditional Ethiopian fermented flatbread
Areki: Traditional Ethiopian spirit
Tej: Traditional Ethiopian honey wine
Tella: Traditional Ethiopian beer
Back slopping: Using a small amount of previous fermentation as starter culture
Yeast and lactic acid bacteria are important in traditional fermentation
slides.notes: Ethiopian traditional fermented products include injera, areki, tej, and tella. These products rely on microorganisms for their unique flavors and textures.

slides.title: 1.5 Genetic Engineering
key_points: Genetic engineering: Process of transferring DNA from one organism into another
Results in genetic modification and production of transgenic organisms
Applications: Pharmaceuticals, gene therapy, transgenic plants and animals
Animal breeding: Selecting for superior traits in growth rate, egg, meat, milk, or wool production
Transgenic animals: Enhanced prolificacy, feed utilization, growth rate, carcass composition, milk production, disease resistance
slides.notes: Genetic engineering has revolutionized livestock production through selective breeding and transgenic technology. Gene transfer is a relatively rapid way of altering the genome of domestic livestock.

slides.title: 1.5 Tissue Culture
key_points: Tissue culture: Method of propagating plants quickly and in large quantity from fragments of tissue
Fragments of tissue transferred to artificial environment where they can survive and function
Cultured tissue may consist of single cell, population of cells, or whole/part of an organ
Plants produced: Palm trees, orchids, bananas, carrots
Advantages: Large quantity of food with desired quality in small area
Important for producing disease-free, high-quality planting material
slides.notes: Tissue culture is an important biotechnology for developing countries, allowing rapid production of uniform, disease-free plants in relatively little area.

slides.title: 1.6 Health and Wellbeing - Antibiotics
key_points: Human drugs produced via transgenic bacteria: Insulin, growth hormone, tissue plasminogen activator
Antibiotics: Complex organic compounds synthesized by microorganisms
Major sources: Bacteria or fungi from soil
Penicillin: Produced by Penicillium fungus, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928
Streptomycin: Produced by Streptomyces (Actinomycete)
Antibiotics can be bacteriostatic (stop reproduction) or bacteriocidal (kill bacteria)
slides.notes: Antibiotics are produced by microorganisms and attack bacteria by disrupting cell wall production or interfering with protein synthesis. Animal cells are not damaged because they lack cell walls.

slides.title: 1.6 Biosensors and Forensic Science
key_points: Biosensors: Devices linking living microorganisms (or their enzymes) with electrodes
Biological reactions converted into electrical currents
Applications: Measure specific components in beer, monitor pollutants, detect flavor compounds
Detect: Glucose, acetic acid, glutamic acid, ethanol, biochemical oxygen demand, pathogens, herbicides, toxins, proteins, DNA
Forensic Science: Examines evidence using blood, saliva, hair, and DNA analysis
Fingerprints: Unique to each individual, do not change throughout life
slides.notes: Biosensors are rapidly developing biotechnology tools for detecting various substances. Forensic science uses DNA analysis and fingerprints to investigate crimes and determine paternity.

slides.title: 1.6 Forensic DNA Analysis
key_points: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): Used as forensic science tool
Variable Number of Tandem Repeat (VNTR) loci analysis
Odds of two random individuals sharing same genetic pattern: ~1 in 10 billion
Used for: Crime investigation, paternity testing
Gel electrophoresis results show DNA patterns of suspects
Bioinformatics widely acceptable in forensic science
slides.notes: DNA analysis in forensic science has become more reliable and easier with computational tools. It is used to identify criminals and determine paternity with high accuracy.

slides.title: 1.6 Biomining (Microbiological Mining)
key_points: Biohydrometallurgy: Use of microbes to extract metals from ores
Thiobacillus ferrooxidans: Chemolithotrophic acidophilic bacterium that oxidizes sulfur
Converts copper sulfide to water-soluble form
Also oxidizes iron from iron sulfide
Combinations of T. ferrooxidans and T. thiooxidans degrade copper and iron ores more rapidly
Leptospirillum ferrooxidans and T. organoparus degrade pyrite (FeS2) and chalcopyrite (CuFeS2)
slides.notes: Biomining uses bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores. Thiobacillus ferrooxidans oxidizes sulfur in sulfide minerals, releasing pure metals like copper, zinc, lead, and uranium.

slides.title: 1.6 Environmental Applications - Solid Waste and Wastewater
key_points: Solid waste treatment: Composting and landfill
Biodegradable material decomposed by fungi, bacteria, and actinomycetes to produce CO2, water, and humus
Landfills generate methane from anaerobic decomposition, used as fuel
Wastewater treatment: Removes undesirable substances and hazardous microorganisms
Primary treatment: Physical removal of floating objects and sedimentation
Secondary treatment: Microbial oxidation (trickling filter or activated sludge process)
Reduces Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)
slides.notes: Wastewater treatment is fundamental to developed societies, reducing waterborne diseases. Secondary treatment involves microbial oxidation to substantially reduce BOD.

slides.title: 1.6 Bioremediation
key_points: Bioremediation: Use of living organisms or their products for detoxification and degradation of environmental pollutants
Also known as biodegradation
Genetically engineered bacteria metabolically breakdown toxic pollutants into harmless compounds
Mercury resistant bacteria: Process metallic mercury into nontoxic compound
Biotransformation: Enzymes modify toxic pollutant by altering its structure
Heavy metals often rendered less toxic by oxidation or reduction reactions
slides.notes: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to clean up environmental pollutants. Genetically engineered bacteria can break down toxic pollutants into harmless compounds, making this an effective waste treatment process.

slides.title: 1.6 Biofuels and Biogas
key_points: Biofuels: Fuel (chiefly ethanol) obtained by fermentation of plant material
Crop residues: Cellulose and hemicellulose (polymers of glucose, xylose, mannose, galactose, arabinose)
Saccharomyces cerevisiae engineered to ferment xylose
E. coli strain expressing Zymomonas mobilis genes ferments all sugars
Biogas: Combustible gas from anaerobic breakdown of organic matter
Three communities of anaerobic microbes: Eubacteria (first two groups) and Methanogens (Archaea)
Methanogens produce methane: CO2 + 4H2 → CH4 + 2H2O and CH3COOH → CH4 + CO2
slides.notes: Biofuels and biogas are renewable energy sources produced by microorganisms. Biogas is mostly methane and can be used for cooking and lighting, with slurry left for soil conditioner.

slides.title: 1.7 Industrial Applications of Enzymes
key_points: Enzymes produced by commercial fermentation using Aspergillus (fungi) or Bacillus (bacteria)
Selected organisms are non-pathogenic and do not produce antibiotics
Extracellular enzymes: Filtered from feedstock
Intracellular enzymes: Organisms crushed and enzymes extracted
Proteases: Washing powders, cheese manufacture, tenderising meat
Lipases: Flavor enhancer in cheese, washing powders for fatty stains
Pectinases: Clarification of fruit juices
Amylases: Production of glucose from starch
slides.notes: Enzymes have various commercial applications in food, textile, and cleaning industries. Biological washing powders contain proteases and lipases that work at lower temperatures.

slides.title: 1.8 Agricultural Applications - Biopesticides
key_points: Biopesticides: Biological agents to kill susceptible insects
Bacteria: Bacillus thuringiensis (wide variety of crops), Bacillus popilliae (Japanese beetle larvae)
Pseudomonas fluorescens: Contains toxin-producing gene from B. thuringiensis, used on maize
Viruses: Nuclear polyhedrosis virus (NPV), Granulosis virus (GV), Cytoplasmic polyhedrosis virus (CPV)
Fungi: Beauveria bassiana (Colorado potato beetle), Metarhizium anisopliae (sugarcane froghopper)
Verticillium lecanii and Entomophthora spp. (aphids)
slides.notes: Biopesticides use bacteria, fungi, and viruses to control pests. They are considered harmless to humans and reduce the need for chemical pesticides.

slides.title: 1.8 Ti Plasmid and Transgenic Crops
key_points: Ti plasmid: Tumor-inducing plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Used as vector to introduce transgenes into plants
Glyphosate resistance gene inserted into Ti plasmid with antibiotic resistance gene
Construct re-inserted into A. tumefaciens bacterium
Plant cells exposed to transgenic bacterium and cultured on antibiotic plate
Only cells that took up plasmid grow (others killed by antibiotic)
Insect-resistant crops: Maize (corn borer), Cotton (boll weevil)
BT-Cotton: Bacillus thuringiensis genes inserted for insect resistance
slides.notes: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used as a vector to introduce genes into plants. Insect-resistant crops like BT-Cotton produce proteins toxic to insects, improving yield.

slides.title: 1.8 Transgenic Plants and Animals
key_points: Transgenic plants: Received recombinant DNA from other species
Traits: Disease resistance, herbicide/pesticide resistance, better nutritional value, better shelf life
Transgenic animals: Modified to express recombinant DNA
Human proteins expressed in milk of transgenic sheep and goats
Some proteins expressed in eggs of chickens
Mice used for expressing and studying recombinant genes and mutations
Extensive testing required for ecological stability
slides.notes: Transgenic plants and animals are closely monitored by government agencies to ensure they are fit for human consumption and do not endanger other plant and animal life.

slides.title: 1.8 Cloning
key_points: Cloning: Method of producing identical copies of genes, cells, or organisms
Products of cloning called a clone
Clone: Group of genetically identical organisms or cells
Produced either by asexual reproduction or artificially by cloning techniques
Main advantage: Large numbers of plants or animals with desirable characteristics
First successful reproductive cloning of adult: Dolly the sheep
Dolly cloned using somatic cell nuclear transfer
slides.notes: Cloning produces identical copies of organisms with desirable characteristics. Dolly the sheep was the first successfully cloned mammal from an adult cell.

slides.title: 1.9 Biological Warfare
key_points: Biological warfare (BW): Use of biological toxins or infectious agents
Agents: Bacteria, viruses, and fungi
Intent: Kill or incapacitate humans, animals, or plants as an act of war
Biological weapons include any microorganism or toxin found in nature
Bioterrorism: From hoax to actual use of biological weapons
Agents may be used for isolated assassination or mass casualties
Contamination creates long-term threat to population
slides.notes: Biological warfare is the use of biological toxins or infectious agents to harm people, animals, or plants. There are concerns that terrorist groups may acquire these destructive agents.

slides.title: Chapter 1 Summary
key_points: Biotechnology: Application of scientific knowledge to produce biological products
Yeasts, moulds, and bacteria are important industrial microorganisms
Fermentation: Process by which sugar is converted into alcohol and CO2 by yeast
Tissue culture: Propagating plants from tissue fragments in artificial environment
Genetic engineering: Transfer of genes from one organism to an unrelated species
Wastewater treatment: Removal of undesirable substances and hazardous microorganisms
Biogas: Produced by methanogenic bacteria from waste matter
Transgenic plants: Obtained using Agrobacterium tumefaciens plasmid
Bioremediation: Using living organisms to decrease environmental pollutants
slides.notes: Chapter 1 covers the diverse applications of biology in food processing, agriculture, medicine, environmental management, and industry. Biotechnology plays a central role in these applications.

slides.title: Unit 2 Overview - Microorganisms
key_points: Microbiology: Study of microbes, which can only be observed with microscopes
Microorganisms include: Fungi, Bacteria, Algae, Protozoa, and Viruses
Some eukaryotic microorganisms are visible without magnification
Based on evolutionary lines, organisms grouped into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya
Microorganisms play roles as producers and decomposers
slides.notes: Microorganisms are very diverse and found in all three domains of life. They include both prokaryotes (Bacteria and Archaea) and eukaryotes (fungi, algae, protozoa).

slides.title: 2.1 Eubacteria - Introduction
key_points: Eubacteria: 'True bacteria' - relatively simple in structure
Prokaryotic, unicellular organisms
No nuclear membrane, mitochondria, Golgi bodies, or endoplasmic reticulum
Reproduce by asexual division
Omnipresent: Found in soil, air, and water
Cell bears thick rigid cell wall (peptidoglycan) outside plasma membrane
Mode of nutrition: Autotrophic or heterotrophic (parasitic, saprophytic, symbiotic)
slides.notes: Eubacteria are true bacteria with simple cellular structure. They lack membrane-bound organelles and have a peptidoglycan cell wall. They are found everywhere on Earth.

slides.title: 2.1 Bacterial Cell Structure
key_points: Bacteria studied under electron microscope due to minute size
Structures external to cell wall: Flagella, Pili, Glycocalyx (capsule/slime layer)
Structures internal to cell wall: Cell membrane, Cytoplasmic matrix
Cytoplasmic matrix contains: Ribosomes, Inclusions, Nucleoid/Chromosome, Actin cytoskeleton
Some bacteria form endospores for survival
Eukaryotic microbes: Have complex membranous organelles, nucleus, cytoskeleton
slides.notes: Bacterial cells have external appendages, a cell envelope, and internal structures. Eukaryotic microbes have complex organelles and a cytoskeleton for shape and movement.

slides.title: 2.1 Bacterial Shapes
key_points: Bacteria classified based on: Cell shape, Nature of multi-cell aggregates, Motility, Spore formation, Gram stain reaction
Three main shapes:
- Cocci (spherical)
- Bacilli (rod-shaped)
- Spirochaetes (spiral or corkscrew-shaped)
- Comma: Vibrio cholerae
Clustering patterns: Diplococci, Streptococci, Staphylococci, Sarcinae
slides.notes: Bacterial morphology is important for classification. Bacteria can be grouped by their shape and how they cluster together, which helps in identifying species.

slides.title: 2.1 Gram Staining
key_points: Gram-positive: Retain purple crystal violet stain
Thick peptidoglycan layer in cell wall
Examples: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Listeria
Gram-negative: Lose crystal violet stain, take red counterstain
Thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane
Gram staining process: Heat fix → Crystal violet → Gram's iodine → Decolorization → Counterstain (Safranin)
Differential staining distinguishes organisms based on staining properties
slides.notes: Gram staining is a fundamental technique for distinguishing bacteria based on cell wall composition. The difference in staining is due to the thickness of the peptidoglycan layer.

slides.title: 2.1 Nutritional Types of Bacteria
key_points: Autotrophs: Obtain carbon from inorganic CO2
Photoautotrophs: Energy from sunlight
Chemoautotrophs: Energy from inorganic chemicals
Heterotrophs: Obtain carbon from organic molecules
Photoheterotrophs: Energy from sunlight
Chemoheterotrophs: Energy from organic molecules
Phototrophs: Light as energy source
Chemotrophs: Energy from oxidation of chemical compounds
Lithotrophs: Use reduced inorganic substances as electron source
Organotrophs: Extract electrons from reduced organic compounds
slides.notes: Bacteria have evolved various nutritional strategies to acquire energy and nutrients. Most bacteria studied are either photolithoautotrophic or chemoorganoheterotrophic.

slides.title: 2.1 Reproduction in Bacteria
key_points: Asexual reproduction: Binary fission
Process: Chromosome replicates → DNA molecules separate → Cell divides at midcell
Results in two genetically identical daughter cells
Sexual reproduction (Genetic recombination): Conjugation
Conjugation: Two cells of different mating types come together
F+ (donor) cells: Have F factor (fertility) DNA sequence
F- (recipient) cells: Receive DNA through conjugation bridge
Sex pili: Long hair-like extensions that recognize and bind to F- cells
slides.notes: Most bacteria reproduce by binary fission, an asexual process. Genetic variation can occur through conjugation, where DNA is transferred between cells through a sex pilus.

slides.title: 2.1 Common Bacterial Diseases
key_points: Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis (Gram-negative rod) - Upper respiratory tract - Airborne
Meningococcal Meningitis: Neisseria meningitidis (Gram-negative diplococcus) - Meninges - Airborne
Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Acid-fast) - Lungs, bones - Airborne
Typhoid Fever: Salmonella typhi (Gram-negative rod) - Intestine, blood - Food/water
Cholera: Vibrio cholerae (Gram-negative rod) - Intestine - Food/water
Tetanus: Clostridium tetani (Gram-positive spore-forming anaerobic rod) - Nerves - Soil
Syphilis: Treponema pallidum (Spirochete) - Skin, cardiovascular - Sexual
Gonorrhea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gram-negative diplococcus) - Urethra, cervix - Sexual
Leprosy: Mycobacterium leprae (Acid-fast) - Skin, bones, peripheral nerves - Contact
slides.notes: Bacteria cause a wide range of diseases in humans. Understanding the causative agent and mode of transmission is essential for prevention and treatment.

slides.title: 2.2 Archaea
key_points: Archaea: Unicellular, microscopic, prokaryotic organisms
Lack membrane-bound nucleus and organelles
Cell walls lack true peptidoglycan
Cell membrane lipids have branched hydrocarbon chains
Many found in extreme environments
Three major groups: Methanogens, Extreme Halophiles, Extreme Thermophiles
Methanogens: Strictly anaerobic, degrade organic molecules to methane
Extreme Halophiles: Obligate aerobes, grow in highly saline environments
Extreme Thermophiles (Hyperthermophiles): Found near volcanic vents, optimum temperatures >80°C
slides.notes: Archaea are distinct from bacteria in their evolutionary history, genetics, metabolism, and cell wall/membrane composition. They thrive in extreme environments.

slides.title: 2.2 Beneficial Aspects of Archaea
key_points: Source of enzymes for detergents: Maintain activity at higher temperature and pH
Proteases and lipases: Used as detergent additives to increase stain removal
Bioremediation potential: Help clean contaminated sites
Thermus aquaticus: Source of enzyme used in Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
Physical factors affecting microbial growth:
- Solutes and water activity, pH, temperature, oxygen level, pressure, radiation
slides.notes: Archaean enzymes have commercial uses in detergents. Thermus aquaticus is essential for PCR, a fundamental molecular biology technique.

slides.title: 2.3 Fungi - Introduction
key_points: Fungi: Eukaryotic organisms, spore-bearing, absorptive nutrition, lack chlorophyll
Reproduce sexually and asexually
Mycology: Scientific study of fungi
Mycotoxicology: Study of fungal toxins
Mycoses: Diseases caused by fungi
All fungi are eukaryotic
Most are filamentous (composed of hyphae forming mycelium)
Some are unicellular (e.g., yeasts)
Cell wall composed primarily of chitin and glucans
All are chemoheterotrophic (use pre-existing organic sources)
slides.notes: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that absorb nutrients from their environment. They play important roles in decomposition and form symbiotic relationships with plants.

slides.title: 2.3 Fungal Characteristics and Ecology
key_points: Nutritional categories: Saprophytic, Parasitic, Symbiotic
Found in cool, dark, moist places with decaying material
Saprobes: Decompose organic matter
Mycorrhizal associations: Mutualistic relationships with plant roots
Lichens: Symbiotic relationship between fungus and photosynthetic organism (alga or cyanobacterium)
Photosynthetic organism provides energy and carbohydrates
Fungus supplies minerals and protection
slides.notes: Fungi have colonized nearly all environments and form various ecological relationships. They are essential for nutrient cycling and form mutualistic associations with plants and algae.

slides.title: 2.3 Classification of Fungi
key_points: Five major groups (current classification):
Zygomycota: Sporangial fungi (e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor)
Ascomycota: Ascospore-producing fungi (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
Basidiomycota: Basidia-producing fungi (e.g., Rusts, Smuts)
Chytridiomycota: Zoospore-producing fungi (e.g., Allomyces, Water molds)
Glomeromycota: Mycorrhizal fungi
Ethiopian traditional fermented foods: Enjera, Kocho, Bulla, Tej, Shameta
slides.notes: Fungi are classified into five major groups based on their reproductive structures and life cycles. Some fungi are important in Ethiopian traditional fermentation.

slides.title: 2.3 Reproduction in Fungi
key_points: Sporulation: Process of spore formation
Occurs in fruiting bodies (asexual or sexual structures)
Asexual reproduction:
- Sporangiospores: Produced in sporangia
- Conidia: Produced on conidiophores
- Arthrospores: Formed by fragmentation of hyphae
- Budding: In yeasts, producing blastospores
Sexual reproduction:
- Opposite mating types fuse
- Heterokaryon: Cell with genetically dissimilar nuclei
- Nuclei fuse (diploid cell formed)
- Meiosis returns to haploid state
- Results in visible fruiting bodies (e.g., mushrooms)
slides.notes: Fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually. Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical spores, while sexual reproduction creates genetic variation.

slides.title: 2.3 Economic Importance of Fungi - Benefits
key_points: Beneficial aspects:
Decomposers: Recycle carbon and other elements
Food: Edible mushrooms (Basidiomycetes)
Fermentation: Essential for bread, wine, beer, cheese production
Traditional Ethiopian foods: Enjera, Tela(Farsoo), Tej(Dadhii), Bulla
Commercial production: Organic acids (citric, gallic), drugs (ergometrine, cortisone)
Antibiotics: Penicillin, griseofulvin
Immunosuppressive drug: Cyclosporin
Research tools: Studying complex eukaryotic events (cancer, aging)
slides.notes: Fungi are economically important as decomposers, food sources, and for producing fermented foods, organic acids, antibiotics, and drugs. They are also valuable research tools.

slides.title: 2.3 Economic Importance of Fungi - Harmful Aspects
key_points: Major cause of plant diseases: Over 5,000 species attack crops
Deterioration of manufactured goods: Fabrics, leather, electrical insulation
Spoilage of agricultural produce: Vegetables, fruits, cereals
Mycotoxicoses: Ingestion of fungal toxins
- Aflatoxins: Produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus
Carcinogenic, especially in liver
Contaminate peanuts, grains, cereals, corn, rice
- Ergotism: Caused by Claviceps purpurea (ascomycete fungus)
Produces sclerotium containing alkaloids (ergot)
Mycetismus: Mushroom poisoning
Superficial fungal infections: Dermatomycoses/Tineas (ringworm, athlete's foot)
slides.notes: Fungi cause significant economic losses through plant diseases, spoilage of goods, and mycotoxin contamination. They also cause various superficial infections in humans.

slides.title: 2.3 Superficial Fungal Infections
key_points: Superficial mycoses: Infections of hair, fingernails, toenails, and outermost skin layers
Caused by Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, and Microsporum
Referred to as tineas or 'ringworm'
Types: Tinea corporis (ringworm), Tinea pedis (athlete's foot), Tinea capitis (scalp), Tinea barbae (beard), Tinea unguium (nails)
Transmission: Direct human contact, animal-human contact, or indirectly on inanimate objects
Prevention: Regular disinfection of showers and wardrobes
slides.notes: Superficial fungal infections are common and transmitted through contact. Prevention involves good hygiene and avoiding sharing personal items.

slides.title: 2.4 Protozoa
key_points: Protozoa: Unicellular, eukaryotic, chemoorganotrophic protists
Characteristics:
- Unicellular, eukaryotic, aerobic
- Lack cell wall
- May be free-living or parasitic
- Locomotion: Pseudopodia, flagella, cilia, direct cell movements
- Nutrition: Autotrophic, heterotrophic, or saprozoic
- Reproduction: Asexual (fission, budding, cysts) and sexual (conjugation or syngamy)
Classification: Amebae, Flagellates, Ciliates, Sporozoa
slides.notes: Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotes that can be free-living or parasitic. They reproduce both asexually and sexually and are classified based on their means of locomotion.

slides.title: 2.4 Classification of Protozoa
key_points: Ciliates: Move via cilia, reproduce by transverse fission and conjugation, have micronuclei and macronuclei
Examples: Balantidium coli, Paramecium, Stentor, Tetrahymena, Vorticella
Amebae: Move via pseudopodia, reproduce by binary fission
Examples: Amoeba, Naegleria, Entamoeba histolytica
Flagellates: Move via flagella, reproduce by binary fission
Examples: Chlamydomonas, Giardia lamblia, Trichomonas, Trypanosoma
Sporozoa: Generally non-motile, reproduce by multiple fission
Examples: Plasmodium, Toxoplasma gondii, Cryptosporidium
slides.notes: Protozoa are classified into four groups based on their means of movement and reproductive methods. Ciliates have both micronuclei and macronuclei.

slides.title: 2.4 Reproduction in Protozoa
key_points: Asexual reproduction:
- Fission: Cell divides evenly to form two new cells
- Budding: Cell divides unevenly
- Multiple fission (schizogony): Nucleus divides multiple times before cell divides
Sexual reproduction (Ciliates):
- Conjugation: Two individuals exchange haploid micronuclei
- Genetic variation results without reproduction
Binary fission: Asexual reproduction during which macronucleus disintegrates and new one forms
Macronucleus controls everyday cell functions
slides.notes: Protozoa reproduce asexually through fission, budding, or multiple fission. Sexual reproduction occurs through conjugation, especially in ciliates, where genetic material is exchanged.

slides.title: 2.4 Common Diseases Caused by Protozoa
key_points: Amoebiasis: Entamoeba histolytica (Intestine, liver) - Ingestion of contaminated food/water
Giardiasis: Giardia lamblia (Intestine) - Ingestion of contaminated water
Trichomoniasis: Trichomonas vaginalis (Urogenital organs) - Sexual contact
African sickness (Sleeping sickness): Trypanosoma brucei (Blood, brain) - Tsetse fly vector
Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar): Leishmania donovani (White blood cells, skin, intestine) - Sand fly vector
Malaria: Plasmodium spp. (Liver, red blood cells) - Anopheles mosquito vector
Toxoplasmosis: Toxoplasma gondii (Blood, eye) - Domestic cats, food
slides.notes: Protozoa cause some of the most important human diseases, many of which are transmitted by insect vectors. Malaria is one of the most serious protozoan diseases worldwide.

slides.title: 2.5 Viruses - Introduction
key_points: Virus: Very small, non-cellular parasite of cells
Genome: Composed of either DNA or RNA, enclosed in protein coat
No cellular organelles, cannot carry out metabolic processes
Must enter other cells to reproduce
Obligate intracellular parasites
Most can only be seen with electron microscope
Lack chemical machinery for generating energy and synthesizing large molecules
Must find appropriate host cell to replicate
slides.notes: Viruses are acellular infectious agents that require a host cell to replicate. They are composed of nucleic acid and a protein coat, and cannot carry out metabolic processes independently.

slides.title: 2.5 Characteristics and Structure of Viruses
key_points: Characteristics:
- Inner core of nucleic acid surrounded by protein coat
- Cannot be grown on artificial cell-free media
- No cellular organization (no cell wall, membrane, or organelles)
- Obligate intracellular parasites
- Unaffected by antibacterial antibiotics
- Inert (nucleoprotein) filterable agents
- Occupies space between living and non-living
Structure:
- Core: Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) - Genome
- Capsid: Protein coat surrounding core
- Nucleocapsid: Combined core and capsid
- Envelope: Glycoprotein and phospholipid bilayer (in some viruses)
slides.notes: Viruses have a simple structure of nucleic acid core and protein coat. Some viruses have an outer envelope. They lack the machinery for protein synthesis and must hijack host cells.

slides.title: 2.5 Viral Symmetry and Classification
key_points: Viral Symmetry:
Helical: Protein subunits assemble in helix around genome (Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Sendai virus)
Icosahedral: 20-sided polyhedral structure (Papovavirus, Picornavirus, Adenovirus, Toga virus)
Complex: Complicated structures (Pox virus, Bacteriophages)
Classification:
Based on type of nucleic acid (DNA virus or RNA virus)
DNA viruses: Mostly double-stranded, replicate in nucleus
RNA viruses: Mostly single-stranded, replicate in cytoplasm
Retrovirus: RNA virus with reverse transcriptase (HIV)
Bacteriophage: Virus that infects bacteria
slides.notes: Viruses have three main shapes: helical, icosahedral, and complex. They are classified based on their nucleic acid type and replication strategy.

slides.title: 2.5 Viral Replication - Lytic Cycle
key_points: Five steps in replication: Adsorption, Penetration, Synthesis, Maturation, Release
Lytic Cycle (Virulent phages):
1. Adsorption: Attachment of virus to host cell
2. Penetration: Entry of viral genome into host cell
3. Synthesis: Viral components produced using host machinery
4. Maturation: Assembly of new virions
5. Release: Lysis of host cell, releasing new phages
Enzyme lysozyme breaks down cell wall, allowing viruses to escape
T4 phages: Example of virulent (lytic) phages
slides.notes: The lytic cycle results in the destruction of the host cell and release of new phage particles. This is characteristic of virulent phages that infect bacteria.

slides.title: 2.5 Viral Replication - Lysogenic Cycle
key_points: Lysogenic Cycle (Temperate phages):
Viral DNA integrates into host genome (prophage)
Prophage replicates along with host DNA
Host cell divides normally without lysis
Under certain conditions, prophage may enter lytic cycle (induction)
Lysogenic bacterium: Carries prophage within its genome
Lysogenic vs Lytic:
- Lytic: DNA doesn't integrate, host DNA hydrolyzed, no prophage stage, fast
- Lysogenic: DNA integrates, host DNA not hydrolyzed, prophage stage, slow
slides.notes: Temperate phages integrate into the host chromosome as a prophage and replicate with it. Under certain conditions, they may enter the lytic cycle and cause cell lysis.

slides.title: 2.5 Common Viral Diseases
key_points: Mumps: Mumps virus - Swollen salivary glands - Droplet contact - Vaccine
Measles (Rubeola): Measles virus - Cough, fever, rash - Droplet contact - Vaccine
Rabies: Rabies virus - Fever, paralysis, hydrophobia - Bite from rabid animals - Avoid rabid animals
Polio: Polio virus - Often no symptoms - Fecal-oral route - Polio vaccine
Common cold (Rhinitis): Rhinoviruses, Adenoviruses - Sneezing, sore throat - Respiratory droplets - Good hygiene
Chickenpox (Varicella): Varicella-zoster virus - Fever, itchy rash - Droplet contact - Chickenpox vaccine
slides.notes: Viruses cause many common and serious diseases in humans. Vaccination and good hygiene are important prevention methods.

slides.title: 2.6 Normal Microbiota
key_points: Normal microbiota: Population of microorganisms routinely found on healthy individuals
Resident microbiota: Microbes that inhabit body sites for extended periods
Transient microbiota: Temporary occupants
Protective roles:
1. Cover binding sites that pathogens might use
2. Consume available nutrients
3. Produce compounds toxic to other bacteria
4. Stimulate adaptive immune system
Disruption (e.g., by antibiotics) can allow pathogens to cause disease
Example: Oral antibiotics can cause overgrowth of Clostridium difficile (antibiotic-associated diarrhea)
slides.notes: The normal microbiota protects against pathogens and stimulates the immune system. Understanding its role helps explain infections when it is disrupted by factors like antibiotics.

slides.title: 2.6 Koch's Postulates
key_points: Germ Theory of Disease: Diseases caused by microorganisms
Koch's Postulates: Rigorous criteria to link specific microorganism to specific disease
1. Disease-causing organism must always be present in diseased animals, not in healthy ones
2. Organism must be cultivated in pure culture away from animal body
3. Isolated organism must cause disease when inoculated into healthy susceptible animals
4. Organism must be isolated from newly infected animals and cultured again, same as original
slides.notes: Koch's postulates provide a framework for proving that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease. They have been fundamental in medical microbiology.

slides.title: 2.7 Modes of Disease Transmission
key_points: Four main routes in healthcare settings: Contact, Droplet, Airborne, Common vehicle
Droplet infection: Respiratory diseases (Common cold, 'flu, pneumonia)
Drinking contaminated water: Cholera, typhoid fever
Eating contaminated food: Salmonellosis, typhoid fever, listeriosis, botulism
Direct Contact: Athlete's foot, ringworm
Sexual intercourse: Candidiasis, syphilis, AIDS, gonorrhoea
Blood-to-blood contact: AIDS, hepatitis B
Animal vectors: Malaria (mosquitoes), sleeping sickness (tsetse flies)
slides.notes: Understanding disease transmission routes is essential for prevention and control of infectious diseases in healthcare and community settings.

slides.title: 2.8 Uses of Microorganisms
key_points: Agriculture: Organic matter decomposition, humus formation, nitrogen fixation
Nitrogen fixation: Only bacteria can convert atmospheric nitrogen to usable form
Sewage treatment: Anaerobic bacteria reduce sludge volume, produce methane gas
Bioremediation: Microorganisms degrade environmental contaminants
Food production: Lactic acid bacteria produce yogurt, pickles, cheeses, sausages
Medicine: Production of human insulin using recombinant DNA technology
Health: E. coli aids digestion and synthesizes vitamins (biotin, vitamin K, folic acid)
slides.notes: Microorganisms have diverse applications in agriculture, waste treatment, medicine, and food production. They are essential for nutrient cycling and human health.

slides.title: 2.8 The Carbon, Nitrogen, and Phosphorus Cycles
key_points: Carbon cycle:
- Carbon fixation by primary producers (photosynthesis)
- Respiration and fermentation release CO2
- Methanogenesis: CO2 reduced to methane by archaea
- Methane oxidation: Methane oxidized to CO2
Nitrogen cycle:
- Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobia form symbiosis with legumes in root nodules
Phosphorus cycle:
- Organic P in soils (microbial origin)
- Inorganic P (orthophosphates) mostly as aluminum, iron, or calcium compounds
slides.notes: Microorganisms are essential for biogeochemical cycles. They convert elements into forms usable by plants and animals and are responsible for decomposition and nutrient recycling.

slides.title: 2.9 Controlling Microorganisms
key_points: Sterilization: Freed of all living microorganisms (vegetative and spore state)
Germicide (Microbicide): Any chemical agent that kills pathogenic microorganisms
Disinfection: Destroys or removes pathogenic organisms (not endospores) from inanimate objects
Antisepsis: Application of chemical agents to living tissue to destroy or inhibit vegetative pathogens
Sanitization: Mechanical removal of microorganisms (reduces contaminants)
Preservation: Prevents microbial spoilage of susceptible products
Decontamination: Removal or reduction of microorganisms contaminating an object
slides.notes: Various terms describe different levels of microbial control. Sterilization is the most absolute, while sanitization reduces contaminants to safe levels.

slides.title: 2.9 Physical Methods of Sterilization
key_points: Pasteurization: Antimicrobial treatment for liquids
- Low-temperature: 61.5°C, 30 minutes; 71°C, 15 seconds
- High-temperature: Brief exposure to 80-85°C
- Uperization: 150°C for 2.5 seconds
Dry heat sterilization:
- Flaming: Holding in flame until red hot
- Incineration: Burning to ashes (for infectious waste)
- Hot air oven: 160-180°C for 2 hours
Moist heat sterilization (Autoclaving):
- 121°C, 15 minutes, one atmosphere pressure
- 134°C, 3 minutes, two atmospheres pressure
Intermittent sterilization (Tyndallization):
- 100°C for 20 minutes on three consecutive days
slides.notes: Heat is a simple and effective method for sterilization and disinfection. Different methods are used depending on the material and required level of sterilization.

slides.title: 2.10 Bacterial Isolation Techniques
key_points: Microorganisms isolated from food, soil, water, or other materials
Process:
1. Sample collection from desired sites
2. Serial dilution: Separating microorganisms on artificial media
3. Purification: Each isolate purified on new media
4. Characterization: Morphological characteristics (shape, gram nature, arrangement, motility)
5. Biochemical characterization: Testing enzymatic activities
6. Molecular techniques: Further identification
slides.notes: Isolating microorganisms involves collecting samples, diluting them, and growing them on artificial media. Characterization includes morphological and biochemical tests, with molecular techniques for final identification.

slides.title: 2.11 Renowned Microbiologists in Ethiopia
key_points: Activity: Search for and study the works of renowned microbiologists/parasitologists in Ethiopia
Evaluate the contribution of their research to the world of science
slides.notes: This section encourages students to research and appreciate the contributions of Ethiopian scientists in the field of microbiology and parasitology.

slides.title: Chapter 2 Summary
key_points: Microorganisms found in all three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya
Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes (lack cellular nucleus)
Archaea differ from bacteria in evolutionary history, genetics, metabolism, and cell wall/membrane composition
Eukaryotes studied in microbiology: Algae, Protozoa, Fungi, Helminths
Algae: Plant-like, unicellular or multicellular, derive energy via photosynthesis
Protozoa: Unicellular, complex cell structures, most are motile
Microscopic fungi: Molds and yeasts
Helminths: Multicellular parasitic worms (eggs and larvae are often microscopic)
Viruses: Acellular, require a host to reproduce
slides.notes: Chapter 2 provides a comprehensive overview of microorganisms, their characteristics, classification, reproduction, and importance. It covers bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, viruses, and normal microbiota.

slides.title: Unit 3 Overview - Energy Transformation
key_points: Living cells require energy for macromolecule assembly, transport, and genetic transmission
Metabolism: Enzyme-mediated chemical reactions in living matter
Energy transformations occur through catabolic and anabolic reactions
Photosynthesis: Converts light energy to chemical energy stored in sugars
Cellular respiration: Harvests energy from glucose to produce ATP
ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) is the energy currency of cells
slides.notes: This unit explores how cells extract energy from their environment and use it to carry out life activities. Energy transformations are essential for movement, growth, development, and reproduction.

slides.title: 3.1 Cellular Metabolism
key_points: Metabolism: Sum of all chemical reactions within each cell of an organism
Catabolism: Breakdown of complex molecules to release energy
- Exergonic (energy-releasing) reaction
- Occurs during cellular respiration
Anabolism: Synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones
- Endergonic (energy-absorbing) reaction
- Occurs during photosynthesis
Catabolic pathways provide energy needed for anabolic pathways
Cells produce energy for vital processes and synthesize new organic materials
slides.notes: Cellular metabolism consists of catabolic reactions that break down nutrients to release energy and anabolic reactions that use energy to build larger molecules. These processes are interconnected and essential for life.

slides.title: 3.2 Introduction to Photosynthesis
key_points: Photosynthesis: Series of chemical reactions using light energy to assemble CO2 into glucose and other carbohydrates
Chemical equation: 6 CO2 + 12 H2O --(light, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6 O2 + 6 H2O
Provides food for plants and energy, raw materials, and oxygen for heterotrophs
Primary source of atmospheric oxygen
Contributes to the carbon cycle and symbiotic relationships
Photoautotrophs: Plants, multicellular algae, some protists, Cyanobacteria, Purple sulfur bacteria
slides.notes: Photosynthesis is the fundamental process by which solar energy is converted to chemical energy. It is the primary source of food and oxygen for most life on Earth.

slides.title: 3.2 External and Internal Structure of Leaf
key_points: Leaf has three main parts: Leaf base, leaf lamina, and petiole
Epidermis: Continuous layer on outside, one cell thick, provides protection
Cuticle: Waxy coating that helps retain water and protect from drying out
Stomata: Pores allowing entry of CO2 for photosynthesis
Mesophyll: Specialised parenchyma cells between lower and upper epidermis
- Palisade mesophyll: Near upper surface, more chloroplasts
- Spongy mesophyll: Many large air spaces between cells
slides.notes: Leaves are specialized organs for photosynthesis. Their flat shape maximizes surface area for light absorption, and internal structures optimize gas exchange and light capture.

slides.title: 3.2 Structure of Chloroplast
key_points: Chloroplasts: Highest density in mesophyll cells of leaves
Double membrane: Outer and inner membrane
Stroma: Fluid-filled matrix where light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) occur
Thylakoids: Disk-shaped compartments, contain photosynthetic pigments
Grana: Stacks of up to 100 thylakoids
Thylakoid lumen: Interior of thylakoid, site of light-dependent reactions
Intergranal lamellae: Tubular extensions joining thylakoids in adjacent grana
slides.notes: Chloroplasts are the organelles where photosynthesis occurs. They have internal membranes (thylakoids) that contain chlorophyll for light absorption and a fluid matrix (stroma) for carbon fixation.

slides.title: 3.2 Photosynthetic Pigments
key_points: Pigments: Chemical compounds that absorb certain wavelengths of visible light
Chlorophylls: Greenish pigments containing porphyrin ring
- Chlorophyll a: Found in all plants, algae, cyanobacteria
- Chlorophyll b: Found in green algae and plants
- Chlorophyll c: Found in Chromista and dinoflagellates
Carotenoids: Red, orange, or yellow pigments (accessory pigments)
- Carotene: Gives carrots their color
- Fucoxanthin: Brown pigment in brown algae and diatoms
Phycobilins: Water-soluble pigments in Cyanobacteria and Rhodophyta
slides.notes: Photosynthetic pigments absorb light energy of specific wavelengths. Different pigments absorb different parts of the spectrum, allowing plants to capture more solar energy.

slides.title: 3.2 Absorption Spectrum
key_points: Absorption spectrum: Graph showing absorption at different wavelengths
Chlorophyll a: Absorbs violet-blue and reddish orange-red wavelengths
Chlorophyll b: Absorbs mostly blue and yellow light
Neither absorbs green light (reflected, so leaves appear green)
Carotenoids: Absorb in blue-green region of the spectrum
Transfer absorbed energy to (bacterio)chlorophylls
Only absorbed light (largely blue and red) is useful in photosynthesis
slides.notes: The absorption spectrum shows which wavelengths of light are absorbed by different pigments. Chlorophyll a and b absorb blue and red light, while green light is reflected.

slides.title: 3.2 Light-Dependent Reactions - Non-cyclic Photophosphorylation
key_points: Occur in thylakoid membranes (grana)
Use photosystem II (P680) and photosystem I (P700)
Electrons from water used to reduce NADP+ to NADPH
ATP generated via chemiosmosis
Oxygen released as by-product (photolysis of water)
Products: O2, NADPH, ATP
Photolysis: 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e-
Electrons pass through electron transport chain (plastoquinone, cytochromes, plastocyanin)
slides.notes: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation involves both photosystems and produces ATP, NADPH, and O2. It is the primary pathway for generating energy carriers for the Calvin cycle.

slides.title: 3.2 Light-Dependent Reactions - Cyclic Photophosphorylation
key_points: Uses only Photosystem I (P700)
Electrons are cycled back to the photosystem
Only ATP produced; no NADPH or O2 generated
Provides additional ATP needed for the Calvin cycle
Comparison:
- Non-cyclic: First electron donor = Water, Last electron acceptor = NADP, Products = ATP + NADPH + O2
- Cyclic: First electron donor = Photosystem I (P700), Last electron acceptor = Photosystem I, Products = ATP only
slides.notes: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces only ATP. It occurs when the cell needs extra ATP to drive the Calvin cycle, without producing NADPH.

slides.title: 3.2 Calvin Cycle (Light-Independent Reactions)
key_points: Occurs in stroma of chloroplast
Uses ATP and NADPH from light-dependent reactions
Three stages: Fixation, Reduction, Regeneration
Fixation: CO2 combines with RuBP (5-carbon) → 3-PGA (3-carbon)
- Catalyzed by Rubisco
Reduction: ATP and NADPH convert 3-PGA to G3P
Regeneration: Some G3P forms glucose, others recycled to RuBP
Requires 12 NADPH2 and 18 ATPs to fix 6CO2 into one hexose sugar
slides.notes: The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 into carbohydrates using energy from ATP and NADPH. It consists of three stages: fixation, reduction, and regeneration of the CO2 acceptor.

slides.title: 3.2 C3, C4, and CAM Plants
key_points: C3 Plants: First product is 3-carbon compound (PGA)
- Examples: Wheat, rye, oats, orchard grass
- ~95% of plants on Earth
C4 Plants: First product is 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetic acid)
- Examples: Maize, sugarcane, sorghum
- Fix CO2 using PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells
- Reduce photorespiration by spatial separation
CAM Plants: Stomata open at night, close during day
- Examples: Cacti, succulents
- Reduce water loss by temporal separation
slides.notes: Plants have evolved different carbon fixation pathways to adapt to different environments. C4 and CAM plants minimize photorespiration and water loss.

slides.title: 3.2 Photorespiration
key_points: Photorespiration: Oxidation of organic compounds by oxygen in presence of light
RuBisco combines with O2 instead of CO2
Releases CO2 but does not produce ATP
Considered wasteful process
Occurs in C3 plants (common), reduced in C4 plants, absent in CAM plants
Substrate: Glycolate
Also called photosynthetic C-oxidation cycle or glycolate pathway
CO2 compensation point: CO2 concentration where uptake equals release
slides.notes: Photorespiration is a wasteful process where RuBisco uses O2 instead of CO2. C4 and CAM plants have evolved mechanisms to minimize this process.

slides.title: 3.3 Contributions of Photosynthesis
key_points: Primary source of oxygen in the atmosphere
All food comes directly or indirectly from photosynthesis
Fossil fuels represent remains of organisms that relied on photosynthesis
Carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen atoms are recycled through photosynthesis
Removes CO2 from atmosphere (inhibits global warming)
Provides energy for life through food chains
Oxygen produced is used for aerobic respiration and ozone formation
slides.notes: Photosynthesis is essential for life on Earth. It produces oxygen, is the basis of food chains, and helps regulate atmospheric CO2 levels.

slides.title: 3.4 Introduction to Cellular Respiration
key_points: Cellular respiration: Process by which cells produce energy (ATP) from glucose
ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate): Energy currency of the cell
ATP structure: Adenine + Ribose + 3 phosphate groups
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy: ATP → ADP + Pi + energy
Coupled reactions: Energy from exothermic reactions drives endothermic reactions
Example: ATP hydrolysis + muscle contraction
ATP can be recycled: AMP ↔ ADP ↔ ATP
slides.notes: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose and stores it in ATP molecules. ATP is the universal energy currency that powers cellular processes.

slides.title: 3.4 Stages of Aerobic Respiration
key_points: Four stages: Glycolysis, Pyruvate Oxidation, Krebs Cycle, Oxidative Phosphorylation
Glycolysis: Cytoplasm, no oxygen required
Pyruvate oxidation: Mitochondrial matrix
Krebs cycle: Mitochondrial matrix
Oxidative phosphorylation: Inner mitochondrial membrane
Summary equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP
Prokaryotes: All stages in cytoplasm
Eukaryotes: Glycolysis in cytoplasm, rest in mitochondria
slides.notes: Aerobic respiration has four stages that occur in different cellular locations. It produces more ATP than anaerobic processes.

slides.title: 3.4 Glycolysis
key_points: Occurs in cytosol, anaerobic condition
Common pathway for both aerobic and anaerobic respiration
Glucose (6C) → 2 Pyruvate (3C)
Three phases: Energy investment, Cleavage, Energy liberation
Energy investment: 2 ATP used
Energy liberation: 4 ATP produced, 2 NADH produced
Net yield: 2 ATP, 2 NADH
Net reaction: Glucose + 2ADP + 2NAD+ + 2Pi → 2Pyruvate + 2ATP + 2NADH + 2H+ + 2H2O
slides.notes: Glycolysis is the first stage of glucose breakdown. It produces a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH, which can be used in later stages of respiration.

slides.title: 3.4 Pyruvate Oxidation (Link Reaction)
key_points: Occurs in mitochondrial matrix
Pyruvate (3C) → Acetyl CoA (2C)
Three-step process:
Step 1: Carboxyl group removed → CO2 released
Step 2: Hydroxyethyl group oxidized → NADH produced
Step 3: Acetyl group transferred to CoA → Acetyl CoA formed
Overall: 2Pyruvate + 2NAD+ + 2CoA → 2Acetyl-CoA + 2NADH + 2H+ + 2CO2
slides.notes: Pyruvate oxidation links glycolysis to the Krebs cycle. It converts pyruvate to Acetyl CoA, releasing CO2 and producing NADH.

slides.title: 3.4 Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle)
key_points: Occurs in mitochondrial matrix
Acetyl CoA (2C) combines with OAA (4C) → Citric acid (6C)
Series of reactions release energy and CO2
For each Acetyl CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP/ATP, 2 CO2
For 2 Acetyl CoA (from one glucose): 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP, 4 CO2
Regenerates OAA (4C) for next cycle
Also called Citric Acid Cycle
slides.notes: The Krebs cycle completes the oxidation of glucose, producing energy carriers (NADH, FADH2) and releasing CO2. It runs twice for each glucose molecule.

slides.title: 3.4 Oxidative Phosphorylation
key_points: Occurs in inner mitochondrial membrane
Major source of ATP in aerobic organisms (26 out of 30 ATP)
Three major steps:
1. Electron transfer through electron transport chain (ETC)
2. Generation of proton gradient across inner membrane
3. ATP synthesis via ATP synthase (chemiosmosis)
ETC complexes: FMN, Coenzyme Q, Cytochromes
NADH: 3 ATP per molecule
FADH2: 2 ATP per molecule
slides.notes: Oxidative phosphorylation is the most productive stage of cellular respiration. It uses the energy from electrons to create a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis.

slides.title: 3.4 Energy Yield from Glucose
key_points: Total yield: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP
From one glucose: 2 NADH (glycolysis), 2 NADH (pyruvate oxidation), 6 NADH (Krebs), 2 FADH2 (Krebs), 2 ATP (substrate-level)
NADH: ~3 ATP each → ~18 ATP total
FADH2: ~2 ATP each → ~4 ATP total
Substrate-level ATP: 4 ATP (2 from glycolysis + 2 from Krebs)
Total theoretical yield: ~36-38 ATP per glucose
Actual yield: ~30-34 ATP
slides.notes: The complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yields approximately 36-38 ATP. This high efficiency makes aerobic respiration the preferred energy pathway for most organisms.

slides.title: 3.4 Energy from Non-Carbohydrate Sources
key_points: Proteins: Digested to amino acids, deaminated, enter glycolysis or Krebs cycle
- Deamination: Removal of amino group → ammonia/urea
Fats: Digested to glycerol and fatty acids
- Glycerol → G3P (enters glycolysis)
- Fatty acids → Acetyl CoA via beta oxidation
- Beta oxidation: Breaks fatty acids to 2-carbon fragments
Fats produce more than twice as much ATP per gram as carbohydrates
Excess amino acids cannot be stored; deaminated and used for energy
slides.notes: Cells can use proteins and fats for energy when carbohydrates are unavailable. Fats are particularly energy-rich, storing more energy per gram than carbohydrates.

slides.title: 3.4 Fermentation (Anaerobic Respiration)
key_points: Occurs in absence of oxygen
Recycles NAD+ from NADH to allow glycolysis to continue
Only glycolysis occurs: Net yield 2 ATP
Alcohol fermentation (yeast):
- Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde + CO2
- Acetaldehyde + NADH → Ethanol + NAD+
Lactic acid fermentation (muscles, bacteria):
- Pyruvate + NADH → Lactic acid + NAD+
Facultative anaerobes: Can undergo fermentation when oxygen is absent
slides.notes: Fermentation allows glycolysis to continue in the absence of oxygen by regenerating NAD+. It produces only 2 ATP per glucose and produces either ethanol or lactic acid as by-products.

slides.title: Chapter 3 Summary
key_points: Metabolism: Sum of chemical reactions; includes catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis)
Photosynthesis: Light reactions in grana, Calvin cycle in stroma
Light reactions: Produce ATP, NADPH, and O2
Calvin cycle: Fixes CO2 into carbohydrates
C3, C4, and CAM plants: Different adaptations for carbon fixation
Cellular respiration: Glycolysis → Pyruvate oxidation → Krebs cycle → Oxidative phosphorylation
Fermentation: Anaerobic, produces 2 ATP per glucose
ATP is the energy currency of cells
slides.notes: Chapter 3 covers the processes by which cells transform energy. Photosynthesis captures energy from sunlight, while cellular respiration releases energy from glucose to produce ATP.

slides.title: Unit 4 Overview - Evolution
key_points: Evolution: Change in genetic composition of population over successive generations
Caused by meiosis, hybridization, natural selection, or mutation
Leads to divergence of populations and origin of new species
Various theories explain the origin of life on Earth
Evidence for evolution comes from multiple scientific fields
slides.notes: This unit explores the definition of evolution, various theories of origin of life, evidence supporting evolution, and mechanisms driving evolutionary change.

slides.title: 4.1 Theories of Origin of Life - Special Creation and Spontaneous Generation
key_points: Special Creationism: Life created by supernatural or divine force
- Linked to different religious interpretations
- Not supported by scientific evidence
Spontaneous Generation (Abiogenesis): Life arises spontaneously from non-living matter
- Disproved by experiments:
- Francesco Redi (1668): Maggots from fly eggs, not rotting meat
- Lazzaro Spallanzani: Sealed flasks remained sterile
- Louis Pasteur: Swan-neck flasks disproved theory
slides.notes: Early theories of life's origin include special creation and spontaneous generation. Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments conclusively disproved spontaneous generation.

slides.title: 4.1 Theories of Origin of Life - Eternity, Cosmozoan, and Biochemical
key_points: Eternity of Life: Life has always existed, no beginning or end
- Linked to steady-state theory of the universe
Cosmozoan Theory (Panspermia): Life brought to Earth from elsewhere
- Richter (1865): Spores from meteorites
- Helmholz (1884): Protoplasm from meteorites
Biochemical Origin (Oparin-Haldane Theory):
- Organic molecules from inorganic materials in reducing atmosphere
- Energy from UV radiation
- Coacervate droplets (pre-cells) formed
- Miller-Urey experiment: Produced amino acids from simple gases
slides.notes: The biochemical origin theory is supported by experimental evidence. The Miller-Urey experiment showed that organic molecules could form spontaneously under conditions thought to exist on early Earth.

slides.title: 4.1 Early Life and Autotrophs
key_points: First organisms: Prokaryotes (~4 billion years ago)
Likely had RNA as genetic material
Gave rise to three lines: Archaebacteria, Eubacteria, Eukaryotes
Shift from reducing atmosphere to oxygen atmosphere (~2.4 billion years ago)
Chemoautotrophs: Energy from inorganic chemicals, CO2 as carbon source
- Found in extreme environments
Photoautotrophs: Light energy, CO2 for photosynthesis
- Cyanobacteria responsible for oxygen increase
slides.notes: Early life consisted of prokaryotes that evolved into three domains. The evolution of photosynthesis by cyanobacteria led to the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere.

slides.title: 4.1 Lamarckism
key_points: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744-1829)
Theory of Inheritance of Acquired Characters (1809)
Four postulates:
1. New Needs: Environmental changes create new needs
2. Use and Disuse: Organs used more become larger/developed; organs not used become reduced
3. Inheritance of Acquired Characters: Favorable acquired traits passed to offspring
4. Speciation: Accumulation of new characters leads to new species
Example: Giraffe neck elongation
Significance: First comprehensive theory of evolution
slides.notes: Lamarck proposed that organisms can pass on traits acquired during their lifetime. This theory has been disproved by genetics, as acquired characteristics are not inherited.

slides.title: 4.1 Darwinism (Theory of Natural Selection)
key_points: Charles Darwin (1809-1882)
Voyage on HMS Beagle: Galapagos Islands finches
Influenced by Alfred Russell Wallace and Charles Lyell
Basic Postulates:
1. Geometric increase: More offspring produced than can survive
2. Struggle for existence: Competition for limited resources
3. Variation: No two individuals are exactly alike
4. Natural selection: Advantageous variations survive and reproduce
5. Origin of species: Accumulation of variations leads to new species
'Descent with modification'
slides.notes: Darwin's theory of natural selection explains how species evolve through the differential survival and reproduction of individuals with advantageous traits. This is the driving force of evolution.

slides.title: 4.1 Neo-Darwinism
key_points: Modern synthesis: Combines Darwin's theory with genetics
Incorporates knowledge of genes, alleles, and gene pools
Gene pool: All alleles available in a population
Postulates of Neo-Darwinism:
1. Genetic variability: Mutations create new alleles
2. Natural selection: Acts on phenotype, affects allele frequencies
3. Reproductive isolation: Prevents gene flow between populations
Explains evolution in terms of changes in allele frequencies
slides.notes: Neo-Darwinism integrates Darwin's theory of natural selection with genetics. It explains evolution as changes in allele frequencies within populations over time.

slides.title: 4.1 Evidence for Evolution - Comparative Anatomy
key_points: Homologous structures: Same basic anatomy, different function
- Indicate common evolutionary origin
- Example: Forelimbs of mammals (human arm, whale flipper, bat wing, cat leg)
- Pentadactyl limb: Five digits in all
Analogous structures: Same function, different anatomy
- Indicate different evolutionary origins
- Example: Wings of birds, bats, and insects
Vestigial organs: No longer in use
- Example: Human tailbone (coccyx), appendix
slides.notes: Comparative anatomy provides evidence for evolution. Homologous structures indicate common ancestry, while analogous structures show convergent evolution.

slides.title: 4.1 Evidence for Evolution - Embryology and Fossils
key_points: Embryology: Similarities in embryonic development
- Vertebrate embryos have gill slits and tails early in development
- Indicates common ancestor
Fossils: Preserved remains or impressions of once-living organisms
- Types: Bones, teeth, footprints, burrows, coprolites
- Stratigraphy: Relative dating from rock layers (strata)
- Radiometric dating: Absolute dating using radioactive isotopes
- Half-life: Time for half of radioactive atoms to decay
slides.notes: Comparative embryology and the fossil record provide strong evidence for evolution. Fossils show how organisms have changed over time, and dating methods determine their ages.

slides.title: 4.1 Evidence for Evolution - Biochemistry
key_points: Comparing DNA, RNA, and proteins between species
More closely related species share more similar sequences
Humans share 98% of DNA with chimpanzees
Hemoglobin comparisons:
- Lamprey: One polypeptide chain
- Most animals: Four chains
- Differences in amino acid sequences indicate divergence
Molecular clock: Rate of mutation in genes is relatively constant
slides.notes: Comparing DNA and proteins provides molecular evidence for evolution. The degree of similarity reflects the relatedness of organisms and their divergence from common ancestors.

slides.title: 4.1 Types of Natural Selection
key_points: Directional Selection: Favors one extreme phenotype
- Population average shifts towards that extreme
- Example: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria
Stabilizing Selection: Favors intermediate phenotypes
- Selects against extremes, reduces variation
- Example: Human birth weight
Disruptive Selection: Favors both extremes
- Selects against intermediate, leads to two distinct groups
- Example: Birds with very large or very small beaks
Antibiotic resistance: Modern example of natural selection
slides.notes: Natural selection can act in different ways on populations. Directional, stabilizing, and disruptive selection each have different effects on phenotype distributions.

slides.title: 4.1 Patterns of Evolution
key_points: Divergent Evolution: Two species become increasingly different
- Example: Pentadactyl limb in different mammals
- Responsible for current diversity of life
Convergent Evolution: Unrelated species evolve similar traits
- Example: Wings of birds and insects
- Due to similar environmental pressures
Parallel Evolution: Unrelated species evolve in similar ways
- Without occupying the same niche
slides.notes: Different patterns of evolution occur depending on environmental pressures and relationships between species. Divergent evolution creates diversity, while convergent evolution creates similarities.

slides.title: 4.1 Speciation
key_points: Allopatric Speciation: Geographic isolation
- Physical barrier separates populations
- Populations evolve independently
- Example: Galapagos finches
Sympatric Speciation: No geographic isolation
- New species evolves within same area
- Often due to reproductive isolation
- Example: Polyploidy in plants
Key factors: Isolation, mutation, selection pressures, reproductive isolation
slides.notes: Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated. Allopatric speciation involves geographic separation, while sympatric speciation occurs without it.

slides.title: 4.1 Reproductive Isolating Mechanisms
key_points: Prezygotic Barriers (prevent fertilization):
- Ecological/Habitat isolation: Different habitats
- Temporal isolation: Different reproductive times
- Behavioral isolation: Different courtship behaviors
- Mechanical isolation: Incompatible reproductive structures
- Gametic isolation: Gametes incompatible
Postzygotic Barriers (prevent viable/fertile offspring):
- Hybrid inviability: Embryo dies early
- Hybrid sterility: Hybrid survives but infertile (e.g., mules)
- Hybrid breakdown: Second-generation hybrids weak/sterile
slides.notes: Reproductive isolating mechanisms prevent gene flow between species. Prezygotic barriers act before fertilization, while postzygotic barriers act after fertilization.

slides.title: 4.1 Human Evolution - Key Concepts
key_points: Humans and chimpanzees evolved from common ancestor (~6 million years ago)
Hominin: Any member of genus Homo
Hominid: Includes Homo and other related species
Key traits: Bipedalism evolved before large brain
Important fossils:
- Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis): 3.2 million years, bipedal, small brain
- Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus): 4.4 million years, mixed bipedal/arboreal
Both found in Ethiopia (cradle of mankind)
slides.notes: Human evolution is traced through fossil evidence in Africa. Lucy and Ardi are important fossils that show bipedalism evolved before large brains.

slides.title: 4.1 Brain Size and Human Migration
key_points: Brain size increased during human evolution
- Australopithecus: 0.7-1.0% of body mass
- Modern humans: 1.8-2.3% of body mass
- Human brain uses 25% of resting energy
Larger brain enables: Planning, tool use, communication
Modern humans (Homo sapiens): Appeared in Africa (~300,000 years ago)
Migration out of Africa: Started ~120,000 years ago
Adaptations to different environments:
- Shorter, squatter body shape (cold climates)
- Increased adipose tissue (insulation)
slides.notes: Human evolution is characterized by increasing brain size and migration out of Africa. Different populations adapted to local environments through natural selection.

slides.title: 4.1 Mutation - Types and Causes
key_points: Mutation: Permanent change in DNA base sequence
Ultimate source of new genetic variation
Point Mutations (affect single nucleotide):
- Silent: No change in amino acid
- Missense: Changes amino acid
- Nonsense: Creates premature stop codon
Frameshift Mutations (often more severe):
- Addition/Insertion: Extra nucleotides added
- Deletion: Nucleotides removed
Chromosomal Mutations (affect large segments):
- Inversion, Deletion, Duplication, Translocation
slides.notes: Mutations are changes in DNA that create genetic variation. They can be small (point mutations) or large (chromosomal mutations) and can have various effects on protein function.

slides.title: 4.1 Genetic Drift and Gene Flow
key_points: Genetic drift: Random changes in allele frequencies
- Most significant in small populations
- Bottleneck effect: Population size reduced by catastrophe
- Founder effect: Small group colonizes new area
Gene flow (Migration): Movement of alleles between populations
- Immigration: New alleles introduced
- Emigration: Alleles removed
Horizontal gene transfer: Genes between different species (common in bacteria)
slides.notes: Genetic drift and gene flow are mechanisms of evolution. Drift is random and affects small populations, while gene flow transfers alleles between populations.

slides.title: 4.1 Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
key_points: Theoretical state where allele frequencies do not change
Five conditions required:
1. No mutations
2. Random mating
3. No natural selection
4. Extremely large population size
5. No gene flow
Equations:
- Allele frequencies: p + q = 1
- Genotype frequencies: p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1
p = frequency of dominant allele, q = frequency of recessive allele
p2 = frequency of dominant homozygotes, 2pq = frequency of heterozygotes, q2 = frequency of recessive homozygotes
slides.notes: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is a model that describes conditions under which evolution does not occur. It provides a baseline for measuring evolutionary change.

slides.title: 4.1 Causes of Species Extinction
key_points: Anthropogenic effects: Human activities
- Habitat destruction, deforestation
- Pollution, greenhouse gas emissions
- Overexploitation (hunting, fishing)
- Introduction of invasive species
Natural disasters:
- Volcanic eruptions, asteroid impacts
- Floods, climate changes
Mitigation: Conservation, habitat protection, sustainable resource use
slides.notes: Species extinction is caused by both human activities and natural events. Conservation efforts are essential to prevent further loss of biodiversity.

slides.title: Chapter 4 Summary
key_points: Evolution: Change in genetic composition of populations
Theories of origin: Special creation, Spontaneous generation, Eternity, Cosmozoan, Biochemical
Evidence: Comparative anatomy (homologous/analogous structures), Embryology, Fossils, Biochemistry
Natural selection: Directional, Stabilizing, Disruptive
Speciation: Allopatric and Sympatric
Human evolution: Key fossils (Lucy, Ardi), bipedalism, brain size
Mutation, Genetic drift, Gene flow
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: Conditions for no evolution
slides.notes: Chapter 4 covers the theory of evolution, evidence supporting it, mechanisms driving it, and the origin of species. It emphasizes the importance of natural selection and genetic variation.

slides.title: Unit 5 Overview - Human Body Systems
key_points: Two main coordination systems: Nervous system and Endocrine system
Nervous system: Uses nerve cells to pass electrical impulses
- Stimulates target cells by secreting neurotransmitters
- Rapid, short-duration responses
Endocrine system: Produces hormones transported in blood plasma
- Target cells have specific receptors
- Slower, longer-lasting responses
slides.notes: The nervous and endocrine systems work together to coordinate body functions. The nervous system provides rapid responses, while the endocrine system provides slower, longer-lasting control.

slides.title: 5.1 The Nervous System - Overview
key_points: Central Nervous System (CNS): Brain and spinal cord
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): Nerves outside CNS
Three functions:
1. Sensory input: Receptors detect stimuli, send signals to CNS
2. Information processing: Integration of input in CNS
3. Motor output: Signals from CNS to muscles, glands, organs
Neurons: Basic structural and functional units
slides.notes: The nervous system is divided into the CNS (brain and spinal cord) and PNS (all other nerves). It performs sensory, integrative, and motor functions.

slides.title: 5.1 Neurons - Structure and Function
key_points: Neurons: Basic structural and functional units of nervous system
Three parts:
1. Cell body (Soma): Contains nucleus, organelles
2. Dendrites: Receive signals from other neurons or sensory receptors
3. Axon: Transmits signals away from cell body
Myelin sheath: Fatty insulation, speeds up impulse transmission
- Formed by Schwann cells in PNS
Nodes of Ranvier: Gaps in myelin sheath
Grey matter: Cell bodies (CNS)
White matter: Myelinated axons (CNS)
slides.notes: Neurons are specialized cells that receive, conduct, and transmit signals. Their structure supports their function, with dendrites receiving signals and axons transmitting them.

slides.title: 5.1 Types of Neurons
key_points: Sensory (Afferent) Neurons: Carry impulses from receptors to CNS
- Long dendrite, short axon
- Respond to physical and chemical stimuli (sound, touch, heat, light)
Motor (Efferent) Neurons: Carry impulses from CNS to effectors
- Long axon, short dendrites
- Control voluntary and involuntary movements
Interneurons (Association Neurons): Found entirely in CNS
- Pass signals from sensory to motor neurons
- Integrate functions
slides.notes: Neurons are classified by function into sensory, motor, and interneurons. Sensory neurons bring information to the CNS, motor neurons send commands out, and interneurons process information.

slides.title: 5.1 The Nerve Impulse - Resting Potential
key_points: Resting potential: When axon is not conducting impulse
- Membrane polarized: Outside positive, inside negative (~-65 mV)
- Na+ concentration: 16x higher outside
- K+ concentration: 25x higher inside
- Membrane more permeable to K+ than Na+
Na-K pump: Actively transports
- 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in (uses ATP)
Result: Accumulation of positive ions outside
slides.notes: The resting potential is maintained by differential ion concentrations and the Na-K pump. The inside of the neuron is negative relative to the outside due to K+ leakage.

slides.title: 5.1 The Nerve Impulse - Action Potential
key_points: Action potential: Rapid change in polarity during impulse transmission
Depolarization:
- Voltage-gated Na+ channels open
- Na+ rushes into cell
- Inside becomes positive (+40 mV)
- Lasts ~3 milliseconds
Repolarization:
- Na+ channels close, K+ channels open
- K+ rushes out of cell
- Inside becomes negative again
Na-K pump restores ion concentrations
All-or-nothing response: Threshold must be reached
